summary: ZeroG Flame is an interactive dashboard that answers one question for spacecraft designers and crews: “Is this cabin atmosphere inside the range where we actually have fire-test evidence?” Fire behaves very differently in microgravity: there is no buoyant flow, so flames spread, grow and go out in ways Earth tests do not predict. Future exploration vehicles also plan to use oxygen-enriched, low-pressure atmospheres such as NASA’s Exploration Atmosphere (34% O2 at 8.2 psia). ZeroG Flame checks any cabin atmosphere against measured results from NASA microgravity fire experiments (SAFFIRE-I/III, BASS, FLEX), flags conditions that fall outside the tested range, and lists the relevant findings by hazard: flame spread, extinguishment, material flammability, smoke detection, ignition and test method. It turns scattered research results into a fast, traceable safety check, which matters because a fire is one of the few emergencies where a crew cannot evacuate or wait for help.
details:
What it does
ZeroG Flame is a decision-support dashboard for spacecraft fire safety in microgravity and partial gravity. It brings 28 findings curated from NASA flight experiments and reports into one place and lets engineers check a cabin design against them. It has six pages:

  1. Overview: the 28 findings by hazard (flame spread 9, extinguishment 6, material flammability 5, smoke detection 4, ignition 3, test method 1) and the highest-relevance measured results.
  2. Research: every finding as a card showing what was measured, under which conditions, what it means for a spacecraft, and its source, with search, hazard filters and sorting by safety relevance. Example: in SAFFIRE-I, a 40.6 x 94 cm cotton-fiberglass sample burned completely at 1.8 mm/s with about 1200 W flame power.
  3. Risk Check: users build a mission scenario from a preset (ISS, Exploration, Mars, Shuttle 10.2 psi), then set oxygen, pressure, ventilation, gravity, materials, suppression and smoke detection. The dashboard returns a Mission Fire Brief with an “Outside tested range” flag when applicable, plots the scenario on a flammability map (oxygen vs. air flow speed, with real flight-test points marked burned or did not burn), and lists the top issues to review, each with its NASA evidence and a question for the engineering team. The brief exports to PDF. ZeroG Flame never labels a cabin safe or unsafe; it only says whether flight tests match it.
  4. Ask: plain-language questions answered only from the NASA records, with every claim linked to its record. If the records do not cover a question, it says so.
  5. Compare: up to three tested materials side by side, with a warning when test conditions differ too much for a fair comparison.
  6. Knowledge Gaps: a coverage matrix of gravity (orbit, lunar, Mars) against cabin atmosphere. Only ISS-like air in microgravity has solid-material flight data. Each gap lists what is known, what is missing, why it matters, and a proposed next experiment.

Example: NASA’s proposed Exploration Atmosphere (34% O2 at 8.2 psia; Garbino 2022, NTRS) is flagged “Outside tested range”. Solid-material tests cover only 13.6 to 22.2% O2 at about 1 atm, and the closest evidence is FLEX liquid-droplet tests, a different kind of fire.

Key findings shown to the user

  • A realistic-size cabin fire can sustain itself and release kilowatt-level heat in microgravity (SAFFIRE-I).
  • Ventilation speed controls how fast a fire grows; shutting it down is a key first response (SAFFIRE-I/III).
  • Materials certified safe on Earth may still burn in a spacecraft (BASS).
  • The Earth extinguisher technique may fail or make a fire worse in microgravity (BASS).

How it works
A curated evidence dataset stores each record’s experiment, oxygen, pressure, flow speed, material, outcome, hazard and source. A check step compares the selected atmosphere with the tested conditions and returns a status, the closest evidence and caveats. Charts (flammability map, hazard bars, coverage matrix) present the result in seconds.

Why it matters
Artemis-era and commercial spacecraft will fly new atmospheres and materials. Fire is a top crew-safety risk, and microgravity fire data are rare and scattered. ZeroG Flame makes that evidence searchable and makes the gaps visible, helping designers choose safer atmospheres and materials and showing researchers which tests are still needed.

Tools
The dashboard was built by vibe coding with Claude (Anthropic): the team described each page and feature, Claude wrote the code, and the team tested and refined it. It is hosted on Vercel. The team selected the NASA sources, built the dataset, checked every finding against the original reports, and directed the design.
